lines: A farmer asked for a hoe that never wears out. I asked for a field that weeds itself.
I made a silent hammer once. Nobody could find it.
The miner wanted a lighter pickaxe, so I took the emeralds out of the price.
My first apprentice measured every handle twice and still cut the wrong end.
A shovel walks into the shop. I tell it to stop digging itself deeper.
I offered the butcher a sharpening lesson. He said he preferred learning the hard way.
The grindstone and I agree on everything. It just takes a while to come around.
A farmer returned a bent hoe and blamed the soil. The soil had no comment.
Someone asked whether I talk to my tools. Only the ones that listen.
The bell has one <jump>joke</jump>. It rings and everyone remembers an urgent appointment elsewhere.
I repaired a clock once. It came back a week later, right on time.
A miner asked how long a pickaxe should last. I said longer if you stop using it as a doorstop.
My hammer never loses an argument. It does ruin the table sometimes.
I tried making a square wheel. The cartographer said it would put us on the map.
A good file is patient. It has heard every rough excuse already.
The fisherman brought me a bent hook and a story about a monster. The hook was more convincing.
I keep my jokes beside the scrap metal. Both might be useful one day.
A villager asked for a left-handed wrench. I sent them to the armorer.
The anvil complained about my hammering. I told it to toughen up.
I made an axe for chopping excuses. Business has been excellent.
The mason wanted a softer hammer. I gave him a pillow and kept the emerald.
I sharpened a hoe so well the weeds started packing.
My tools are never late. The people borrowing them are another matter.
A cracked handle said it needed space. I gave it the scrap bin.
I do have a good repair joke, but it works better the second time.
